title: One thing
hookLine: research on multitasking finds switching costs attention and time

lines: AN EMAIL, A PING, A TAB.
cards: An email, half written, on the screen. A message pings, so you answer it. A tab with a news story.
Back to the email: where was I? A calendar reminder. Back again.
At the end of the hour, everything has been touched and nothing is finished. It felt like doing several things at once. The research on task switching suggests you weren't.
You were doing one thing at a time, very fast, and paying a toll at every switch. Today: one thing.

teach.b: In studies of task switching, such as work by Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans, people were slower when they had to switch between tasks than when they stayed with one, and the cost grew as the tasks got more complex.
The mind has to drop one set of rules and pick up another, and that takes time and attention, even when it feels instant. Second, a very old line.
Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible, says, "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." Not with half your might while checking something else.
The Teacher of Ecclesiastes is blunt about how short life is, and this is part of his answer: give the thing in front of you your whole self. Third, a philosopher's version.
The Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard wrote a work known in English as Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing.
For him it went deeper than time management: a divided heart, wanting many things at once, can't fully want anything. One thing at a time, done with a whole heart, became for him a spiritual matter.
Fourth, looking back at this week. Ruskin asked for joy in making. Morris asked for useful work.
Gibran called work love made visible. Levin found the scythe moving on its own. A psychologist named flow.
Each, in its own way, asks for a person present to the thing in front of them, even when that thing is sleep: not doing less, but doing one thing, wholly, and then the next.

how: People who practice single-tasking often set a fixed block of time, close other windows and silence their phones; some also treat it as a form of mindfulness, returning gently whenever attention wanders.

o: doing only the easiest task first, then stopping
doing many tasks at once, quickly and smoothly
giving one task your whole attention, then the next

games.q: who said what about one thing — tap the pairs.
p: purity of heart is to will one thing
the scythe moving on its own

s: when we multitask, we're really doing several things at once
the studies describe switching between tasks, very fast, with a cost at each switch.
in the studies, the cost of switching grew as tasks got more complex
dropping one set of rules and picking up another takes more when the rules are harder.
Kierkegaard treated willing one thing as only a time-management tip
for him it was a matter of the heart: a divided heart can't fully want anything.

games.q: you're writing an email and a message pings. by what the switching studies found, what keeps the toll lowest?
o: answer it right away, then come back.
finish the email first, then answer.
answer it and check the news while you're there.
games.why: every switch costs time and attention. finishing one thing before starting the next pays the toll once instead of over and over.

practice: Choose one thing and stay with it: the feeling of your breath at the tip of your nose.
When your attention switches, to a sound, a plan, an itch, you'll feel the little toll; no need to scold yourself, just switch back, and if you like, count each return on a finger.
The point isn't a perfect score; it's practicing the way back.

wordCard.voice: One thing. Giving a single task your whole attention, because every switch has a cost, and a whole heart can only be given whole. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: practicing the way back. Every return counts, however many it takes. That's day nine hundred ten.
